intro: A closed-end private fund usually lives ten to twelve years on paper and fifteen or more in practice, counting the years before launch and the obligations that survive dissolution. The stages below follow one fund from the first idea to the last record destroyed. Timings are typical for a European or Indian PE/VC fund; individual funds vary.

stages.goal: Build a team, a thesis and a record that LPs will back.
stages.summary: Most funds are decided long before any document is drafted. Founders spin out of an existing manager, a corporate, a family office or an operating career. What they can show at this point (deals they led, results they can prove, people who will follow them) sets the ceiling on what they can raise.
activities: Assemble the core team and agree who will be a key person, who holds carry and how decisions are made
Document an attributable track record: which deals each person sourced, led and sat on the board of, with cash flows
Clear exit terms with any former employer: non-compete, non-solicit, use of track record, unvested carry left behind
Test the thesis with deals done personally, through SPVs, angel investing or a pledge fund
Speak informally to potential anchors, without crossing into marketing a specific fund
documents: Track record schedule with deal-level cash flows
Attribution letters or references from former employer
Team term sheet or founders' agreement
people: Early supporters and potential anchor LPs
decisions: Raise a blind pool, or start with deal-by-deal SPVs
Where the team and management company will sit
Who owns the management company and in what shares
kpis: Number of deals with clean attribution
Realised DPI of prior deals
Warm relationships with LPs who back emerging managers
pitfalls: Claiming team credit for deals led by others; LPs check references
Spinning out without settling carry and track record rights in writing
Pitching a specific fund before structure and regulation allow it
compliance: Pre-marketing rules start to bite as soon as a specific fund or its terms are discussed (EU CBDF; Monaco ban on canvassing by unlicensed firms)
Confidentiality and non-solicit obligations to the former employer
Personal investing and conflicts rules if still employed at a regulated firm
refs: ILPA Principles 3.0 on team and alignment
GIPS guidance on portability of track record (CFA Institute)
checklist: Track record built deal by deal and reconciled to cash flows
Former employer consents obtained in writing
Team economics agreed and written down
Thesis tested against real deal flow

stages.goal: Turn the thesis into a fund that works on paper: size, strategy, terms, structure.
stages.summary: The team builds a model of the fund: how many deals, what cheque sizes, reserves, fees and expected returns. From that comes the target size and the terms. Structure and domicile follow from who the LPs will be and where they sit.
activities: Build the portfolio construction model: number of companies, initial cheques, reserves, target ownership, expected loss ratio
Model the management company budget to see what fee income the team needs and whether target size covers it
Benchmark terms against peers: fee rate and basis, carry, hurdle, GP commitment, term, key person, removal
Pick domicile and vehicle to fit the LP base, e.g. Luxembourg SCSp/RAIF for EU LPs, SEBI Cat I/II AIF for Indian LPs, GIFT IFSC for dollar pools, Delaware or Cayman for US and global LPs
Decide whether parallel funds, feeders or blockers are needed
Settle the ESG and SFDR position and whether the fund name uses any ESG term
documents: Term sheet or summary of principal terms
decisions: Self-managed or third-party AIFM / host platform
kpis: Fund model returns 3x gross in the base case for VC (or the strategy's target)
Management fee covers the team's realistic budget
Terms within market range for the strategy and fund number
pitfalls: Setting target size from ambition rather than from the portfolio model
Choosing a domicile your target LPs cannot invest in
Ignoring tax drag on key LP groups until late
compliance: Check investor eligibility rules for the chosen vehicle: e.g. FPCI €100,000 minimum (or €30,000 with conditions); SEBI ₹1 crore per investor unless accredited; IFSCA venture capital scheme USD 250,000 and max 50 investors
Fund names: ESMA guidelines limit ESG and sustainability terms in EU fund names
SFDR disclosure category (Article 6, 8 or 9) under current rules; SFDR 2.0 is still in negotiation
refs: ILPA Model LPA (whole-of-fund and deal-by-deal versions)
ESMA Guidelines on funds' names using ESG or sustainability terms
checklist: Portfolio model agreed by all partners
Structure chart signed off by counsel and tax

stages.goal: Create the legal entities, obtain authorisations and appoint service providers.
stages.summary: Counsel drafts the documents and incorporates the GP, the management company and the fund. The manager secures its licence or joins a host platform. Administrator, depositary or custodian, auditor and bank are appointed. Regulators that register funds review the filing.
activities: Incorporate GP, management company and the fund vehicle; open bank accounts
Obtain or confirm manager authorisation: AIFM licence (CSSF, AMF), CCAF licence in Monaco, SEBI registration of the AIF and filing of the scheme PPM through a merchant banker, IFSCA FME registration
Appoint administrator, depositary or custodian, auditor, legal counsel, and AML officer
Draft LPA, PPM, subscription agreement, IMA, side letter template, valuation policy, conflicts policy
Put compliance policies in place: AML/KYC, conflicts, personal dealing, record keeping, data protection, cybersecurity
decisions: Whether to put a subscription line in place at launch
kpis: Regulatory approvals received on schedule
Documents final before first LP diligence
Service provider fees within budget
pitfalls: Underestimating licensing timelines
Sponsor KYC gaps that delay bank account opening
Valuation and conflicts policies written as boilerplate that later fail LP diligence
compliance: SEBI: sponsor and manager fit and proper; continuing interest planned; compliance officer with NISM certification
EU: AIFM authorisation or appointment of an authorised AIFM; depositary appointed
Monaco: management in or from Monaco needs CCAF authorisation, usually through a SAM
IFSCA: minimum corpus of USD 3 million for VC and restricted schemes, to be reached within 12 months of the PPM being taken on record
refs: Luxembourg AIFM Law of 12 July 2013 as amended by the Law of 3 March 2026 (AIFMD II)
AMF General Regulation Book IV (FPCI declared funds)
checklist: Fund registered or filed where required

stages.goal: Win enough commitments to hold a first close.
stages.summary: The team tests interest, then markets formally once the fund is authorised for the target countries. LPs run investment and operational due diligence. Terms move during negotiation, and side letters accumulate.
activities: Pre-market where allowed: draft terms only, no subscription possible; notify the home regulator within two weeks where EU pre-marketing rules apply
Build the data room: PPM, LPA, track record, team bios, policies, model, references, DDQ
Run roadshow meetings and LP site visits
Answer ILPA DDQ and ODD questionnaires; host LP operational reviews
Negotiate with an anchor; agree side letters and MFN mechanics
File marketing notifications (AIFMD passport, national private placement regimes, Monaco through a CCAF-authorised distributor)
decisions: When to hold first close and at what minimum size
What economics to give an anchor
Which side letter terms to grant and to whom
kpis: Soft circles as a share of target
Conversion rate from meetings to commitments
Time from first meeting to signed subscription
pitfalls: Taking subscriptions from countries where the fund was never notified
Relying on reverse solicitation after pre-marketing has begun (EU 18-month rule)
Granting side letter terms that later trigger expensive MFN elections
compliance: EU CBDF: pre-marketing letter to home regulator within two weeks; any subscription within 18 months of pre-marketing counts as marketing
Monaco: unlicensed firms may not canvass Monaco private residents, solicited or not
US: Regulation D offering rules, SEC Marketing Rule if a registered adviser
Placement agent licensing in each country
refs: Monaco Law 1.529 of 29 July 2022 on marketing
CCAF FAQ on marketing to Monaco residents

stages.goal: Admit the first LPs and switch the fund on.
stages.summary: LPs sign subscription agreements, pass KYC and are admitted. The LPA is executed. The investment period and management fee usually start. The first capital call covers fees, organisational expenses and any warehoused deal.
activities: Collect subscription documents, tax forms and KYC; screen against sanctions lists
Countersign the LPA and admit LPs; issue closing notices
Make regulatory filings due at launch
Issue the first capital call; draw on a subscription line if one exists
Transfer warehoused investments if any, at cost plus agreed carrying charge
decisions: Whether to call capital now or bridge with a facility
kpis: Size at first close as a share of target (often 40–60%)
Days from closing to first call
pitfalls: Admitting an LP with incomplete KYC
Fee start date disputes because the LPA defines first close loosely
compliance: SEBI: scheme cannot hold first close until minimum corpus is met; sponsor or manager continuing interest in place
IFSCA: minimum corpus achieved within the PPM validity window
AML: beneficial owners identified and verified for every LP
refs: SEBI AIF Regulations, Regulation 10 (corpus, minimum investment, continuing interest)
FATF Recommendations on customer due diligence

stages.goal: Fill the fund up to target or hard cap and finish fundraising.
stages.summary: More LPs join at subsequent closes. Each pays equalisation so that it ends up as if it had joined at first close. MFN elections are processed once the final close is done. After the final close the fund is closed to new money.
activities: Hold subsequent closings; calculate equalisation and late-closing interest
Return excess equalisation to earlier LPs
Process MFN elections after final close
Confirm final fund size and update LP percentages
decisions: Whether to use the final close extension if the LPA allows
Whether to accept commitments above target up to the hard cap
kpis: Final size vs target
LP diversification by type and country
Share of commitments from re-up LPs (for later funds)
pitfalls: Late-closing interest set too low, so later LPs get a free option
Missing the final close deadline in the LPA
compliance: New country marketing notifications if adding LP jurisdictions
Investor caps: SEBI 1,000 non-accredited investors per scheme; IFSCA venture capital scheme max 50 investors
refs: ILPA Principles 3.0 on equalisation and MFN

stages.goal: Build the portfolio the PPM promised.
stages.summary: The team sources, diligences and invests, following the portfolio construction plan and the LPA's limits. Capital is called deal by deal or in bundles. Reporting, valuations and LPAC meetings run on a fixed rhythm.
activities: Source and screen deals; run due diligence; take deals to the investment committee
Negotiate term sheets and close investments; call capital
Keep within concentration, geography and asset-type limits; get LPAC approval for conflicts
Value the portfolio quarterly under the valuation policy; audit annually
Report quarterly to LPs using ILPA templates; hold an annual meeting
Monitor key person compliance and team stability
documents: Quarterly reports and capital account statements
kpis: Deployment pace vs plan
Ownership achieved vs target
Reserve ratio
Early TVPI and IRR (treat with caution in years 1–3)
pitfalls: Deploying too fast into one market cycle
Drifting from the stated strategy
Breaching concentration limits through follow-ons
Cross-fund deals without LPAC sign-off
compliance: Investment restrictions in the LPA and, in India, SEBI (25% in one investee for Cat I/II, 50% for LVFs)
AIFMD Annex IV reporting; AIFMD II adds loan origination rules for lending
SEBI quarterly reporting and annual PPM compliance audit
US Form PF and Form ADV for SEC-registered advisers

stages.goal: Help companies grow and protect value.
stages.summary: Board work, follow-on rounds and operational help decide how much value the portfolio creates. The team defends its position through down rounds and restructurings, and keeps valuations honest.
activities: Sit on boards; agree value creation plans and budgets
Decide follow-ons from reserves; exercise pro rata rights
Deal with underperformers: bridge, recapitalise, sell or write off
Track ESG and portfolio KPIs; report to LPs
Mark the portfolio to fair value each quarter
kpis: Revenue and EBITDA growth across portfolio
Share of portfolio marked up vs down
Loss ratio
pitfalls: Spreading reserves evenly instead of backing winners
Holding stale marks
Ignoring governance problems at portfolio level
compliance: Insider information controls for listed holdings
Conflicts when the GP, its affiliates or other funds deal with portfolio companies
SFDR periodic reporting for Article 8/9 funds
checklist: Each company has a written value creation plan

stages.goal: Raise Fund II without short-changing Fund I.
stages.summary: Most LPAs bar the GP from raising a successor fund until a set share of commitments (often 70–75%) is invested or the investment period ends. LPs judge Fund II on Fund I's early results and how the team has behaved.
activities: Check the successor fund restriction in the LPA
Prepare a fresh track record with Fund I marks and any exits
Agree fee offset or step-down on Fund I once Fund II charges fees
Set an allocation policy between funds for new deals
decisions: How to handle deals suitable for both funds
kpis: Re-up rate of Fund I LPs
Fund I DPI at time of raise
pitfalls: Launching Fund II before the LPA allows
Cross-fund investments that favour the new fund
compliance: Conflicts policy and LPAC consent for cross-fund deals
Marketing rules apply afresh for Fund II
refs: ILPA Principles 3.0 on successor funds and allocation

stages.goal: Exit investments at the best value and return cash.
stages.summary: The fund sells companies through trade sales, IPOs, secondary buyouts and secondaries. Proceeds run through the waterfall. Carry starts to flow once LPs are made whole and the hurdle is met, subject to escrow and clawback.
activities: Plan exits two to three years ahead; prepare vendor due diligence
Run sale processes or IPOs; manage lock-ups
Calculate waterfall on each distribution; pay carry into escrow where required
Distribute cash or listed shares in kind
Reduce management fee as the fee base shrinks
kpis: DPI
Net IRR
Exit multiple vs entry
Time to liquidity
pitfalls: Paying carry early under a deal-by-deal waterfall and facing clawback later
Warranty and indemnity exposure after sales
compliance: Market abuse rules on listed shares
Tax withholding on distributions; FATCA/CRS reporting
Waterfall audited and disclosed under ILPA templates
refs: ILPA Reporting Template (carry and waterfall disclosure)
ILPA Capital Call & Distribution Template (from Q1 2027)
checklist: Waterfall model reconciled by administrator and auditor

stages.goal: Deal with the last assets without dragging the fund out.
stages.summary: Few funds exit everything inside the term. The GP uses extensions, then turns to secondaries: LPs sell their interests, or the GP moves remaining assets into a continuation vehicle. LPs push for fee cuts on the tail.
activities: Seek extensions under the LPA (GP discretion, then LPAC or LP consent)
Offer a GP-led secondary or continuation vehicle for remaining assets
Support LP-led secondary transfers
Negotiate reduced or zero fees during extensions
decisions: Extend, sell or move to a continuation vehicle
Price and process for any GP-led deal
kpis: Remaining NAV as a share of commitments
Pricing vs NAV in secondary transactions
pitfalls: Conflicted GP-led deals without independent pricing
Charging full fees on a tail portfolio
compliance: Conflicts: LPAC consent for GP-led deals; ILPA continuation fund guidance
SEBI: tenure extension up to two years with two-thirds investor approval for close-ended Cat I/II
checklist: Independent valuation or fairness opinion obtained

stages.goal: Turn everything left into cash or distribute it, settle liabilities and close the vehicle.
stages.summary: The fund sells or distributes the last assets, pays its debts, runs the final waterfall and checks whether the GP owes any clawback. Final accounts are audited. The vehicle is dissolved and registrations are surrendered.
activities: Sell remaining assets or distribute them in specie
Settle liabilities; set aside reserves for known claims
Run the final waterfall and clawback test; release or apply carry escrow
Final audit and final LP report
Dissolve the vehicle; deregister or surrender the regulatory registration
decisions: Size of reserves for contingent liabilities
Whether to use a liquidating trust for leftover assets
kpis: Final net IRR and TVPI
GP share of profit vs agreed carry rate
pitfalls: Releasing escrow before the clawback test
Under-reserving for warranty or tax claims
compliance: SEBI: one-year liquidation period after tenure; dissolution period with 75% investor consent (max original tenure); unsold assets then distributed in specie; certificate surrendered
SEBI April 2026 amendments and June 2026 circular allow retention of proceeds beyond fund life for pending litigation, regulatory demands or residual expenses, and an Inoperative Fund status
EU: AIFM notifies regulator and depositary; final Annex IV report
refs: SEBI circular of 16 June 2026 on retention of proceeds and Inoperative Fund status

stages.goal: Honour obligations that survive dissolution and keep the record straight.
stages.summary: Dissolution does not end every obligation. LP giveback and GP clawback clauses usually survive for a few years. Indemnities to the GP and to buyers can be called. Tax authorities can audit. Regulators require records to be kept, often for five years or more. And the fund's final numbers become the track record for every future raise.
activities: Keep books and records for the required period (commonly five years: AIFMD, SEC Rule 204-2, SEBI after winding up)
Handle late claims: warranty or indemnity claims from buyers, tax assessments, litigation
Call LP giveback if the LPA allows and claims arise
Release final escrows; pay final carry to vested team members
File final tax returns and K-1 or equivalent statements
Lock the final track record: cash flows, IRR, TVPI, DPI, PME, for use in future PPMs
decisions: Who holds the records and for how long
Whether to fund residual claims from management company or call giveback
kpis: Claims settled within reserves
Records retrievable on request
pitfalls: Losing records when the management company changes administrator
Presenting gross returns in future marketing without net and cash flow support
compliance: Record retention rules apply after the fund ends
Marketing rules govern how the closed fund's track record is shown in later funds (e.g. SEC Marketing Rule: net alongside gross)
AML records retention (FATF standard: at least five years)
refs: GIPS standards for private equity performance presentation
checklist: Retention schedule set and owner named
Giveback and clawback expiry dates diarised
Final track record reconciled to audited cash flows
